title: As if they were present
hookLine: some Chinese homes keep an altar for the ancestors
carry: honor the ancestors as if they were present

lines: A SMALL ALTAR, A ROW OF NAMES.
cards: On a high shelf in a family's living room there's a small altar. Wooden tablets stand on it, each carved or painted with a name: a grandfather, a great-grandmother, names older than anyone in the room.
In front of them, a dish of oranges, a cup of tea, a little bowl of sand with incense sticks standing in it. In the morning someone lights a stick, bows, and says a few words.
On a birthday, a favorite dish appears on the shelf before anyone else eats. In some Chinese homes, this shelf is where the family keeps company with the people it came from.

teach.b: Tradition says honoring the ancestors is older than Confucius. What the Analects shows is his attention to how it's done. It says of him, in Legge's translation: "He sacrificed to the dead, as if they were present."
It doesn't settle what happens to the dead.

teach.h: A BELIEF, OR A WAY OF STANDING?
teach.b: It describes a way of standing before them: with full attention, the way you'd stand if a grandmother walked into the room. Some readers hear a belief that the ancestors are really there.
Others hear reverence that matters whether or not they are. Families can hold both.
Another passage, in paraphrase, says that when people take care with their parents' funeral rites, and keep remembering them long after, the goodness of the whole people grows full again.
So the altar isn't only about the dead.

A child who watches her father bow to a name learns she belongs to a line, that she owes something to people she never met, and that someday she'll be the name on the shelf. Then there are the seasonal days.

At the spring festival of Qingming, families go out to the graves, sweep them clean, pull the weeds, and leave food and flowers. Tomb sweeping is real work, and it ends in a meal. Nobody starts from nothing.
Each of us stands on a long line of people who carried life this far, and remembering them says so out loud.

how: Families who keep Chinese ancestral customs light incense and offer food and tea before tablets bearing the names of their dead, and at Qingming in spring they visit the graves to sweep them, make offerings, and share a meal.

games.q: you're at a family altar for the first time and unsure whether the ancestors are really there. by the Analects, how do you stand before them?
o: only bow if you're sure they're present.
stand as if they were present.
skip it until you've decided what you believe.
games.why: Confucius "sacrificed to the dead, as if they were present": full attention, without settling the question first.

practice: Let one person who came before you step forward: a grandparent, a parent who has died, or, if your family history is hard or unknown, the unnamed people who carried your line this far.
Say their name inside if you know it, and stand before them as if they were present; if you pray, remember them in your prayer.
If a loss feels too heavy to hold alone, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: The ancestors. Those who came before, honored in Chinese tradition at home altars and at the graves, with attention, as if they were present. Today's word.
